notes: Political parties are not permitted in the Maldives in 1970, so the ruling slot 13 holds Ibrahim Nasir's presidential government itself. Real institutions fill 1 (People's Majlis), 10 (Hukuru Miskiiy ulama), 14 (atoll chiefs), 22 (armed forces) and 23 (House of Huraa, as in MD); slot 0 holds the exiled leadership of the United Suvadive Republic. MD 2000 parties (PPM, MDP, Adhaalath, MDA, DRP, Jumhooree) are all anachronistic and not used. Other slots are evocative factions rooted in real milieus: Gan base workers, Maldivian students in Colombo and Cairo, Malé nobility and traders, fishermen, Bohra merchants.

0.name: United Suvadive Republic
0.text:
In 1959 the southern atolls of Addu, Huvadhu and Fuvahmulah broke away from Malé as the United Suvadive Republic under Abdullah Afeef, a notable of Hithadhoo who worked closely with the British at Gan. Nasir's forces crushed Huvadhu in 1962, the republic was dissolved in 1963, and Afeef went into exile in the Seychelles under British protection.

Its loyalists want autonomy for the south, free trade with the outside world, an end to Malé's taxes and monopolies and the closest possible ties with Britain and the Gan base. Silenced at home, they keep a quiet following in Addu, where memories of 1959 and resentment of the capital run deep.

1.name: Raiyyithunge Majlis
1.text:
The People's Majlis, the Maldivian legislature since the first constitution of 1932, endorsed the abolition of the sultanate and the republican constitution in 1968 and nominated Ibrahim Nasir for the presidency. Its members are elected by the atolls and Malé or appointed by the president, and most come from notable families and island elites.

It is conservative and deferential, guarding Islamic law, the standing of Malé's established families and a slow pace of change, while now and then voicing atoll grievances over taxes and the fish trade. Its leverage is constitutional: no president can be nominated without it, and it is the only forum where criticism of Nasir can be heard.

2.name: Majeedhiyya Old Boys
2.text:
Graduates of Malé's Majeedhiyya School and of colleges in Colombo form a small modern-educated elite that now staffs the ministries, Radio Maldives and the schools. They remember the short-lived First Republic of Mohamed Amin Didi in 1953, with its schools for girls and its modernising zeal, and they chafe under Nasir's personal rule.

They want a freer press, an elected and assertive Majlis, an end to the banishment of critics to distant islands, wider education and an economy open to private enterprise. Without a party or a newspaper they work through office talk and private letters; their leverage is that the young republic cannot run without their skills.

3.name: Gan Workers
3.text:
Hundreds of Addu islanders work at the Royal Air Force staging post on Gan, leased to Britain under the 1960 agreement, as clerks, drivers, mechanics, cooks and labourers. They form the only real wage-earning working class in the Maldives, paid on British scales and in daily contact with the outside world.

They seek better pay, recognised workers' committees, social benefits and protection from Malé's taxes and controls, and they want the base to stay. Moderate and pragmatic, they look to British trade unionism rather than revolution, and their leverage is simple: the RAF cannot run Gan without them, and Addu cannot live without their wages.

4.name: Colombo Circle
4.text:
Colombo is the window of the Maldivian world, and the Maldivian students and clerks living there have met Marxism through the city's unions, bookshops and the pro-Moscow Communist Party of Ceylon. A small circle reads Soviet pamphlets, follows the United Front's campaign and argues late into the night about the backwardness of the islands.

They want an end to the rule of Malé's great families, state ownership of the fish trade and shipping, mass education, the emancipation of women and friendship with the Soviet Union. They have no organisation at home, where such views mean banishment; their leverage lies in the day the educated generation comes home.

5.name: Inqilaab
5.text:
Young Maldivian seamen serving on foreign ships and Huvadhu islanders scattered in Colombo after the destruction of Thinadhoo in 1962 form a loose and angry network. In the ports of the Indian Ocean some have met the New Left and the cult of Che Guevara; none of them is known by name in Malé.

They dream of overthrowing Nasir and the Malé oligarchy by force, freeing the southern atolls and handing boats and trade to those who work them. Without weapons, money or structure they are more mood than movement; their leverage lies in southern bitterness and the chance of help from abroad.

6.name: Malé Old Guard
6.text:
Older officials, judges and notables of Malé who never accepted the British lease of Gan, signed in 1960 for thirty years, and who watch Western dress, films and radio seeping in through Colombo and the base. They have no organisation; their opinions are heard after Friday prayers and in the households of senior officials.

They want the Gan agreement ended, foreign influence curbed, stricter Islamic morality laws and a foreign policy turned towards the Arab and wider Muslim world. Suspicious of English-medium schooling and of Nasir's outward-looking projects, they draw their leverage from religious sentiment and the deep conservatism of the capital.

7.name: Cairo Nasserists
7.text:
Since the 1950s Maldivian students have gone to Egypt on scholarships to Al-Azhar and other Cairo schools, and some return admiring Gamal Abdel Nasser: his defiance of Britain at Suez, his Arab socialism and his authoritarian modernisation. They form a small network among teachers and junior officials in Malé.

They want a strong presidency backed by a disciplined state party and security forces, nationalisation of trade and shipping, the closure of the British base at Gan and alignment with the anti-imperialist camp of the non-aligned world. Their leverage is their education, their Arabic and the prestige that Cairo still enjoys across the Muslim world.

8.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat
8.text:
Indian Dawoodi Bohra merchants from Gujarat and Bombay once dominated Malé's import trade, and a few Bohra firms still keep agents in the capital and in Colombo. Their community answers to the Da'i al-Mutlaq in Bombay, Syedna Mohammed Burhanuddin, and as foreigners and Shia Muslims they practise their faith discreetly.

They want security for their trade, credit and property, freedom to worship in private and good relations with the government. Moderate and wholly apolitical, they are tolerated for their commerce in a republic where Sunni Islam is the faith of every citizen; their leverage is the rice, cloth and credit that Malé needs.

9.name: Ahlul Bayt Halqa
9.text:
A tiny clandestine circle of Maldivians who met Twelver Shia teaching while studying or trading in Karachi, Bombay and Basra, meeting in private because open Shia worship is unthinkable in the Sunni republic. It looks to the great clerics of Najaf, and it has no known leader.

Its members long for an Islamic order guided by the learned clergy, the rejection of Western influence and a purer faith than Malé's official Islam allows. Discovery would mean banishment to a remote island; their only leverage is secrecy and the contacts they keep with the wider Shia world through Colombo and the Gulf.

10.name: Hukuru Miskiiy
10.text:
The ulama of Malé's seventeenth-century Friday Mosque, the Hukuru Miskiiy, together with the qazis of the courts, form the religious establishment of the republic. Islam is the state religion, Shafi'i law governs family life and much of public life, and the government appoints the judges, the preachers and the island imams.

They uphold Shafi'i jurisprudence, Friday sermons approved by the state, Quran teaching in every island and obedience to lawful authority. Quietist and loyal, they lend the presidency religious legitimacy in exchange for guardianship of public morals; their leverage is the faith of an entirely Muslim nation.

11.name: Khilaafath Halqa
11.text:
A few young Maldivians returning from religious schools in Pakistan and the Hejaz, together with sympathetic preachers in the atolls, read the pan-Islamist literature that circulates through Karachi and Colombo. They meet quietly in homes and island mosques and have no recognised leader.

They reject both the new republic and the memory of the sultanate as un-Islamic, condemn the British base at Gan and dream of a caliphate binding the islands to a united Muslim world under the Sharia. Isolated and watched by the qazis, they matter only if the official Islam of Malé loses its credibility among the young.

12.name: Islaahee Halqa
12.text:
Maldivian graduates of Al-Azhar and other Egyptian institutions bring home the reformist Islam of the Muslim Brotherhood milieu: Quranic revival joined to modern education. Their most prominent figure, the Azhar-trained scholar Maumoon Abdul Gayoom, is teaching in Nigeria, while others serve as teachers and junior officials in Malé.

They want an Islamic revival through schools, publications and preaching, a government accountable to Islamic ethics and to the Majlis, and an end to arbitrary banishment. Moderate and patient, they oppose both secular drift and Nasir's personal rule; their leverage is learning, eloquence in Arabic and the respect the islands give to scholars.

13.name: Nasir administration
13.text:
Ibrahim Nasir, prime minister under the sultanate since 1957, led the Maldives to full independence from British protection on 26 July 1965 and abolished the monarchy in 1968, becoming president of the Second Republic on 11 November. There are no political parties: power is exercised by Nasir, his ministers and a small circle of trusted officials in Malé.

The government pursues authoritarian modernisation without bloc alignment: membership of the United Nations since 1965, English-medium schools, state control of the fish export trade with Ceylon and a firm grip on the southern atolls. Critics are banished to remote islands; its leverage is control of the state, the armed forces and foreign trade.

14.name: Atholhu Verin
14.text:
Each inhabited atoll is governed by an atoll chief appointed from Malé, with an island chief, the katheeb, in every village. These men collect taxes, supervise the fish trade, lead their communities on state occasions and act as the government's eyes and ears, and many come from long-established local families.

They are conservative, pious and parochial, defending atoll customs, local hierarchies and the island economy of fishing, coconut and coir against both Malé's centralism and outside novelty. Loyal to whoever rules, they quietly carry atoll grievances to the capital; their leverage is their hold over almost every island community in the country.

15.name: Beyfulhun
15.text:
The beyfulhun are the old noble families of Malé, the Didi clans and court lineages that monopolised office under the sultans and still dominate the ownership of trading vessels, island land leases and the import trade. They intermarry with the ruling elite, and Nasir himself comes from this world.

They want secure control of shipping, credit and the Colombo trade, protection of their landholdings and leases on uninhabited islands, and a government that consults them. Wary of both popular reform and Nasir's personal power, they work through marriage, patronage and money; their leverage is that almost nothing in Malé happens without them.

16.name: Viyafaariverin
16.text:
Malé's shopkeepers, boat owners and small merchants, together with atoll traders who carry dried fish to Colombo and bring back rice, sugar and cloth. They chafe under the government's control of the fish export trade and the dominance of a few great houses over shipping and credit.

They want free trade with Ceylon and India, an end to state monopolies and licences, lower duties, a reliable currency and room for private shipping and enterprise. Cautious, pious and unorganised, they gain weight with every new boat and shop; their leverage is the commerce on which the capital lives from one monsoon to the next.

17.name: Reef Keepers
17.text:
Fishermen elders, island chiefs' advisers and a few educated officials in Malé who worry about the reefs on which every island depends. Coral is quarried from the house reefs to build the capital, mangroves are cut, and foreign tuna longliners have begun to work the waters beyond the atolls.

They want limits on coral mining, protection of turtles and bait-fish grounds, a defence of pole-and-line fishing against foreign fleets and nets, and respect for the island customs that govern the reef. Few and unorganised, they speak for an old practical wisdom; their leverage is that every island lives or dies by its reef.

18.name: Masverin
18.text:
The fishermen who crew the sailing dhonis of every atoll make up most of the Maldivian people. Their pole-and-line skipjack catch, dried and smoked as Maldive fish, is the nation's main export, sold through channels controlled from Malé, and a fall in Colombo prices brings hardship to whole atolls.

Island voices among them call for fair prices, credit for boats and gear, cooperatives to break the merchants' hold, schools and clinics in the atolls, and a share of the state's income for those who produce it. They have no union and no party; their leverage is their numbers and an economy that rests on their catch.

19.name: Peking Circle
19.text:
A handful of Maldivian students and clerks in Colombo who follow N. Shanmugathasan's pro-Peking communists, reading the Peking Review and English editions of Mao Zedong's quotations. They quarrel with the pro-Moscow students and see themselves as the only true revolutionaries the islands have produced.

They describe the Maldives as a semi-feudal society ruled by Malé families and tied to British imperialism through Gan, and they call for self-reliance, the seizure of trade and shipping and a revolution of the fishermen in the atolls. In Malé such talk would mean banishment; their only leverage is the ideas they will carry home.

20.name: Dhivehi Qaumiyyath
20.text:
A populist mood more than an organisation, carried by Malé clerks, schoolteachers and atoll notables who exalt the Dhivehi language, the Thaana script and the independence won in 1965. It sees itself as the guardian of national unity after the Suvadive secession and the humiliations of the protectorate.

It wants foreign merchants and Ceylonese and Indian workers kept out, the southern atolls firmly bound to Malé, Dhivehi used in every school and office and national history taught with pride. Loyal to the republic but impatient with the old families and foreign-educated officials, its leverage is patriotic sentiment in the capital.

21.name: Thinadhoo Veterans
21.text:
Men who served in the punitive expedition of February 1962, when Nasir's armed boats crushed the rebellion in Huvadhu atoll and the island of Thinadhoo was razed and emptied of its people. They are proud of having saved the nation's unity by force and contemptuous of anyone who would bargain with the south.

They favour a militarised, unitary state, collective punishment of disloyal islands, the expulsion of foreigners and a cult of the nation above both the old families and the clergy. Small and feared, they matter through their places in the security forces and in any renewed southern unrest.

22.name: Sifain
22.text:
The Maldivian armed forces, descended from the guard of the sultans, are a small body of riflemen based in Malé that answers directly to President Nasir. They carried out the 1962 expedition that crushed the rebellion in Huvadhu atoll, and they serve as ceremonial guard, coastal patrol and the regime's reserve of force.

Officered by men from Malé's established families and loyal to Nasir personally, they are the ultimate guarantee against southern secession or palace intrigue. Their weakness is size and equipment; their leverage is that in a country without parties they are the only organised body of armed men.

23.name: House of Huraa
23.text:
The Huraa dynasty reigned over the Maldives from 1759 until the sultanate was abolished by referendum in 1968 and Sultan Muhammad Fareed Didi was set aside in favour of a republic. Fareed Didi died in 1969, and his family remains in Malé, linked by marriage to the great noble houses that once filled the court.

Royalists regard the sultanate as the natural Islamic order of the islands, with the sultan as protector of the faith and arbiter among the noble families. They have no organisation, but tradition, the old aristocracy and atoll elders who never wanted a republic give them a latent following.
